req90.title: Working Agreements: see which rules a project inherits, overrides and gives its agents

spec.goal:
Problem: an owner's ruling on how work is done (who decides, what waits for him) lives in four places: a binding's persona text, its grants, project knowledge rules, and agents' private memory. Each is set separately, and they disagree. On 2026-11-07 chuongld ruled that the chat agent decides work itself and the persona was changed, but the grants still refused a member's own request (FB-566), so the agent asked the asker to confirm what they had just asked. Two sources, one ruling, and a contradiction found only when it bit.

Value: the owner states a way of working once, and every room, run and master follows that one statement. A contradiction is refused when it is written, not discovered in a thread.

Measured by:
- an owner can say which agreement a run or room followed, and why, from one page, with no document or memory search
- a brief and a grant that disagree on the same act cannot both be saved, so the FB-566 shape cannot recur
- a project's agreement can override a default for one act, for example anyone in the room may agree to epod filings while only thanhnh agrees to sid-desk filings, which binding-wide confirmers cannot express
scopeIn: Inspect current agreement, gate, project context and knowledge mechanisms before choosing the smallest implementation. Integrate REQ-76 profile and per-gate overrides, REQ-13 conventions and REQ-50 retrieval principles without maintaining competing configurations.

Working agreements carry a stable identity, concise rule, applicability/scope, authoritative source, change reason and revision history. Support Forge defaults, explicit project overrides and project-only additions.

A project page with aligned lanes or equivalent explicit model: Forge default → Project override → Effective for agents. Show Inherited, Overridden, Project only and Conflict states. Separate locked core guarantees from configurable agreements.

Selected-rule inspector shows default, exact project change, effective wording, conditions, reason, decision source, revision and actor. Include edit and restore-default actions where authorized. Search and filter rules by state.

Resolve explicit overrides before supplying task context. For conditional agreements, show the condition and whether it applies to the selected task/run. Give agents a concise map and the applicable content through existing retrieval/context paths, respecting prompt budgets.

Record the agreement identities/revisions actually supplied or retrieved for a run through existing provenance mechanisms where possible. Allow a historical run view and distinguish its snapshot from current rules.

Changes apply to future work and notify relevant active runs of applicable changes at a safe continuation point. Preserve which revision applied before and after the update. Refresh existing derivative copies and retrieval surfaces where needed.

Retain provenance and retired revisions. Resolve conflicts through existing agent/master authority routing. Hold only the affected decision or action when resolution is required and continue independent work.

Initial examples are autonomy, proportional verification, release authority, audit cadence and coding conventions. Example billing policies and schedule values in the mockup are illustrative and do not authorize changing any project.

Initial Forge defaults, agreed by the owner on 2026-11-07 (FB-569, FB-570), seeded as the shared Forge layer every project inherits, within the operating loop Product → Delivery → Release → Audit → Product. Each is a term as its name and one short sentence as its default; explanation, examples and anti-patterns sit in details opened on demand:
1. Outcome-driven autonomy: an agent chooses how and completes the goal within its granted authority, calling a person only for a decision beyond it.
2. Proportional verification: verify in proportion to a change's impact, widening the checks only on evidence; never verify beyond what the scope needs.
3. Batch delivery: related work goes in batches of at least one whole issue, checked in scope before it moves on; the full suite and CI run after the push, per batch.
4. Continuous audit: audit on a schedule or on real signals; simplifying, normalising and independent refactors happen there, while what bounds or proves the current fix stays in that fix.
5. Progressive disclosure: show by default what the current task and decision need, open detail on demand, and keep what changes a decision or why something is blocked visible at once.
6. Single source of truth: each decision has one authoritative source; a change updates it and what depends on it, and marks what is retired.
7. Evidence-backed state: state reflects its evidence and tells fixed, verified, released and confirmed on the target environment apart.
8. Continuous improvement: audit gates, prompts and skills too, and remove steps that make work wait or repeat once agents can do it; no process heavier than the work needs.
9. Lean testing: add a test only where it proves behaviour that matters or stops a specific regression the existing tests miss; extend an existing test first, and audit duplicate, stale and implementation-bound tests on a schedule.

Each of the initial defaults records its source (the owner's decision of 2026-11-07, FB-569 and FB-570 for lean testing) and links the existing sources it restates (REQ-12, REQ-79, the project rules) so there is one instruction, not two competing ones. A project may override what is allowed; access and state honesty stay core guarantees.

Lean testing's detail, opened on demand (owner, 2026-11-07, FB-570): no test file by default for each change, helper or branch; table or parameterized cases for one behaviour; tests hold the behaviour callers rely on, not function names or file splits; the audit weighs protected behaviour against upkeep, never a file count or coverage alone, and never deletes in bulk by threshold. The agreement stops new accumulation; auditing the existing suite is separate Audit work that needs evidence first. It works with proportional verification and continuous audit, and adds no manual review gate per test.

criteria.body: On a project, a reader can inspect each current working agreement and see its Forge default, explicit project change and effective result, with Inherited, Overridden, Project only or Conflict status. Locked core guarantees are recognizable.

An authorized editor can create a project-only agreement, override an allowed default and restore inheritance. Only declared changes override the default. Scope/conditions and reason are recorded. Access and immutable core guarantees remain enforced.

Selecting an agreement reveals its original rule, exact override, effective content, applicability, authoritative source, actor and revision. A new Forge default cannot silently erase an explicit project override; incompatible changes are surfaced.

Existing project gate profiles/overrides and content conventions are represented using their authoritative configuration. An edit has one effective result through UI and agent entry points, with no second contradictory configuration.

A fresh agent session on a selected project receives or can follow a concise, task-relevant map to the effective agreements. Retired or overridden text is not presented as a competing current instruction. Changes are reflected through the actual runner/plugin/context path.

Given a project override requiring billing checks for billing changes, a billing task receives that requirement with the inherited batch CI rule. An unrelated UI task retains the default verification rule and is not made to run billing checks. These are isolated validation examples.

For a run, a reader can inspect which agreement identities/revisions were supplied or retrieved and their effective result. Editing current agreements preserves historical provenance and the distinction between received context and checks actually performed.

An applicable change reaches new work and is surfaced to affected active runs at a safe continuation point. A conflict identifies the involved sources and scopes, routes resolution through existing authority, and does not freeze unrelated work or require routine owner approvals.

The page supports searching/filtering agreements, inspecting the selected agreement, viewing history and switching from current rules to a run's recorded context. Layout makes overrides and resulting agent instructions legible without opening every item.

Delivery is demonstrated through the normal project UI and a fresh session on the team's runner/context path, using an inherited rule, scoped override, project-only addition, restoration and historical run. Reuse meaningful existing checks and document remaining gaps. The feature adds no mandatory full-repo reading, per-issue full E2E or per-rule human approval to routine delivery.

A room's persona or brief text and its grants cannot state contradicting rules for the same act: saving one that disagrees with the other on who may agree, decide or confirm that act is refused by name, naming both sources and the act. An agreement that is the single source for that act is read by both.

A project agreement can scope who may agree to an act by its target, not only room-wide: for example, any room member may agree to filings on one project while only one named member agrees to filings on another, within the same binding. The effective rule for a given target is shown and is what the agree door applies.

When the feature ships, the nine owner-agreed Forge defaults (outcome-driven autonomy, proportional verification, batch delivery, continuous audit, progressive disclosure, single source of truth, evidence-backed state, continuous improvement, lean testing) are present as Forge-level agreements: each named by its term with its one-sentence default, its source recorded, and links to the existing sources it restates. The Agreements page shows them, and a fresh session's context can retrieve the ones its task needs; the page never ships empty.

feedback.title: Benchmark retrieval on real Forge data before deciding whether to integrate QMD

route.answer: The benchmark ran on real Forge data (forge-dev 0.4.0-dev.611, 2026-11-08), with frozen eval and held-out queries. Recommendation: keep the current Forge retrieval and do not integrate QMD. Forge hybrid finds the right record in the top 5 for 97.6% of eval queries and all held-out ones, at about 0.7-0.8 s, with no superseded or withdrawn record shown as current. node.owner: Autoflow: SidCorp; Epodsystem: the connecting project's account

One OpenAI-compatible gateway (LiteLLM) for assistant and widget chat, the fast model (memory extraction, rerank, titles) and vision, plus an embeddings endpoint for memory, knowledge, issues and search. Text passes the project's egress policy first. The operator runs the gateway and endpoint and holds the provider accounts; Forge never holds a team's model credentials.

node.owner: The operator (SidCorp): gateway, endpoint, provider accounts
